source.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization under Distribution Shifts
source.authors: Myeongho Jeon; J. Sobotka; Suhwan Choi; Maria Brbic

record.file_problem: Whole paper and appendices are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies weak-to-strong fine-tuning and reports PGR, as in the original, in new settings including distribution shifts, with comparisons to the weak supervisor and ground-truth-trained ceiling.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper's own PGR results for naive weak-to-strong fine-tuning and selected RAVEN results/comparisons. Cited results from other papers are excluded. Table 8 provides corruption-specific ImageNet-C PGR values; the paper also reports extensive comparisons among methods, but not every baseline result is transcribed here.
record.test_reason: The study reruns the original weak-to-strong recipe: AlexNet supervising DINO, fine-tuning on weak labels, with PGR as in Burns et al. It then adds source/fine-tuning distribution shift. It reports that naive W2S PGR collapses or goes negative under shift, which argues V1 needs restating and bears directly on V4. It also compares training changes, including Conf, Boots and ensembling (RAVEN), against naive fine-tuning, which bears on V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude that naive W2S often becomes infeasible under source/fine-tuning distribution shift, sometimes falling below the weak supervisor (11 of 19 ImageNet-C corruptions in Figure 2). They also say existing methods (Conf, Boots, V-sup, Bayes, Co-sup) fail to fix this. They propose RAVEN, which adaptively weights an ensemble of weak models; it beats baselines by over 30% OOD, matches or exceeds them InD, and tends to up-weight the most accurate weak model. Limitations they note: seed-only diversity among weak models, and the choice of weighting scheme.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weak-model pseudo-labels and the original PGR formulation, but extends the setting to distribution shifts and multiple tasks; RAVEN additionally ensembles weak models and learns their weights, with an easy-sample initialization phase.
record.method_sensitivity: PGR changes across distribution-shift corruption types, datasets, task, model pair and the number/configuration of weak models. The paper reports that more weak models improve RAVEN performance with diminishing gains; model-wise weights outperform sample-wise weights.

fits_no_version.finding: RAVEN's learned weights usually go to the weak model that is most accurate on the target. Misses coincide with higher spread in weak-model accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A strong student can identify the most reliable weak supervisor without ground truth.

fits_no_version.finding: Under OOD shift, weak models show much higher accuracy variance across seeds, and weak-model target accuracy correlates strongly with W2S accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Supervisor variance and supervisor target accuracy under shift predict W2S outcome.

record.problems: The distribution-shift evidence includes negative PGR across multiple corruptions. Table 8 reports five-run means and standard deviations; many text and preference-alignment PGR entries in the main tables do not show uncertainty there. Some experiments reuse weak models across repeated runs. The paper notes that weak models differing only by random seed may not capture human annotator diversity.
record.rows_left_out: Did not transcribe the full method-by-method result tables (Tables 1–3, 11–12), all ImageNet-C RAVEN corruption rows from Table 8, the full Table 1 image-task breakdown, or all ablations and diversity configurations (Tables 4–6 and 13–19). Kept the full Table 8 naive PGR corruption sweep, selected RAVEN corruption comparisons, main text-task and preference-task naive/RAVEN comparisons, and all scaling-pair RAVEN entries from Table 20.

untested.parts: Representation-based predictors of PGR; chess and reward-model accuracy tasks. Size variation is limited to a few pairs.
Students exploiting what the supervisor can't check; gains shrinking when weak and strong models err alike.
No general theory of when a student must beat its supervisor; Appendix C only analyses RAVEN's weighting under strong assumptions.
Only image classification; no other non-language modalities.

missing.what: Naive PGR on WILDS OOD image tasks (iWildCam 4.21, Camelyon17 2.47, FMoW −1.26) and ImageNet InD (60.97), DINO ViT-B/8 student
No-shift naive PGR baseline (68.49 averaged; 74.01 without weak fine-tuning) and the Table 7 corruption sweep without weak fine-tuning
Naive PGR for Glass blur (−7.78 ± 0.17), the most negative case
Conf and Boots vs naive PGR in image and text settings
Naive PGR across scaling pairs as primary rows (e.g. GPT2→Llama3.2-1B 3.26, SqueezeNet→DINO 14.22)
Naive PGR with weak models of differing architectures/data sources (avg 1.78 and −2.08)

record.verdict_notes: Tranche is T5 rather than T1: the core claim restates V1 as failing under shift, though the image setup copies the original. RAVEN rows are the authors' own method; they count for V2 only because ensembling weak supervisors is named in V2, so treat them with that caveat. The record's V4 'challenges' label was wrong: negative PGR under shift is what V4 predicts, so it supports V4. The V1 'limits_scope for incomplete recovery' label was dropped, since V1 only requires PGR above 0. r24's value and r31's baseline (4.77) do not match Table 2, which gives 10.88. Preference PGR depends on a GPT-4o judge. Weak models are reused across runs.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests several classification and preference-alignment settings, but not all possible tasks, models, or training stages.
Tests RAVEN and selected comparisons with naive fine-tuning; does not isolate every alternative training change across every setting.
Reports task and model-pair variation and a scaling analysis, but does not systematically vary representations or all supervisor/student sizes.

Tests distribution shift and reports negative PGR under some shifts. It does not test whether gains shrink when weak and strong models err alike or whether students exploit what supervisors cannot check.
The paper gives a theoretical analysis of RAVEN under its assumptions, not a test of general conditions under which a student must beat its supervisor.
Tests image classification; does not establish the effect across other non-language modalities.
